p: The Hebrew says the umbilical cord was not cut. Codex Vaticanus says the breasts were not bound.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Rashi reads the word as 'your navel'
readings.en: your umbilical cord was not cut

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete
readings.en: you did not bind your breasts

why: The Hebrew list follows the order of a birth: the cord, the washing, the salting, the wrapping. A cord that is not cut is the first thing a newborn needs. Codex Vaticanus is a different word or a different reading of the same consonants (shorrekh 'your cord' read as shadayikh 'your breasts' is one explanation), and it fits less well with a baby.
b: No Dead Sea scroll preserves 16:4. Rashi explains the Hebrew word sharrekh as 'your navel' and notes that salting the newborn hardens the flesh (as read on Sefaria, Judaica Press translation).

t: 'To him let it be': a clause Codex Vaticanus lacks
p: The last words of 16:15 are obscure Hebrew, and Codex Vaticanus has nothing at all here.

readings.en: to him let it be / it was his

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete

why: The Hebrew is the only Hebrew witness, and a hard reading is likelier to be original than a smooth omission. Codex Vaticanus may have left out words it could not construe.
b: The Hebrew lo yehi is literally 'to him let it be'. Commentators take it as 'her beauty was his', that is, anyone passing could have her. Others think the text is damaged. No Dead Sea scroll preserves 16:15.

p: The Hebrew text says Aram (Syria). Some commentators propose Edom.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Codex Vaticanus 'daughters of Syria' (Swete)
A reading proposed by commentators in place of Aram

why: The Masoretic Text and Codex Vaticanus agree. In Hebrew the letters resh and dalet look alike, and scribes confused Aram and Edom in other places (2 Samuel 8:12; 2 Chronicles 20:2). Edom makes good sense beside the Philistines, but the best-attested reading is Aram.

a: though he himself did none of these things
t: Who did none of these things?
p: The Hebrew says 'he himself' did none of these things. Codex Vaticanus says the son did not walk in his righteous father's way.

readings.orig: וְהוּא אֶת כָּל אֵלֶּה לֹא עָשָׂה
readings.en: and he, all these things he did not do
readings.plain: though he himself did none of these things

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete
readings.orig: ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ τοῦ δικαίου οὐκ ἐπορεύθη
readings.en: he did not walk in the way of his righteous father
readings.plain: He did not walk in the way of his righteous father

why: The Hebrew has the pronoun 'he' (hu) and does not say whom it means. Many English versions and Block take it as the father of 18:10. Codex Vaticanus has a different construction and makes the son the subject, so the two readings give opposite referents. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text and keeps the pronoun open; see the note at this verse.
b: No Dead Sea scroll preserves chapter 18. Codex Vaticanus at 18:10 also lacks the odd Hebrew word 'ach (see the note at 18:10).

p: The Hebrew says he held back his hand 'from the poor'. Codex Vaticanus says 'from injustice', as in 18:8.

readings.en: from the poor he kept back his hand

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete
readings.orig: ἀπ᾽ ἀδικίας ἀπέστρεψε τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: from injustice he turned his hand

why: 18:8 has 'from injustice' (me'avel in the Hebrew), and a copyist or translator could have made 18:17 match it. But the Hebrew 'from the poor' (me'ani) is the harder reading and the one all Hebrew copies have. The two words are close in form (two of the three letters differ), so some commentators prefer Codex Vaticanus; the Plain keeps the Hebrew.

t: A last call Codex Vaticanus lacks
p: The Hebrew ends 'So turn back and live'. Codex Vaticanus ends at 'says the Lord'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete
readings.en: the verse ends 'I do not wish the death of the one who dies'

why: The Hebrew call matches the chapter's argument and is the only Hebrew reading. Codex Vaticanus may have shortened the end of the chapter.

p: The Hebrew has the plural 'leaders'. Codex Vaticanus has the singular 'the ruler of Israel'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete

why: The poem speaks of two cubs, so the plural fits. Codex Vaticanus singular may mean one ruler or may be a general term for the line.

p: The Hebrew says he 'knew his widows'. The Targum has 'palaces'. Codex Vaticanus has neither.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Rashi reads it of the widows (Judaica Press translation, on Sefaria)
Targum Jonathan (English, as read on Sefaria): 'he laid waste their palaces'; the same Hebrew with 'armenotav proposed by commentators
readings.en: and he knew (that is, ravaged) his strongholds

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete
readings.en: and he ranged in his boldness

why: The Plain keeps the Hebrew words. The Hebrew 'widows' (almenotav) has the suffix 'his', while the next line says 'their cities', and a change of one letter gives 'armenotav, 'his palaces', which goes naturally with 'cities'. The Targum's 'palaces' agrees with that reading, but it is an interpretive Aramaic rendering and not a Hebrew manuscript, and no Hebrew manuscript is cited here for the change. Codex Vaticanus has no word for either.
b: Rashi takes 'knew' in its sexual sense: the lion raped the widows and killed their husbands. No Dead Sea scroll preserves chapter 19. See the note at this verse.

a: like a vine in your blood
p: The Hebrew says the vine was 'in your blood', which is hard. Codex Vaticanus reads 'like a flower on a pomegranate'.

readings.en: like a vine in your blood
readings.plain: like a vine in your blood

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed in Swete
readings.orig: ὡς ἄμπελος καὶ ὡς ἄνθος ἐν ῥόᾳ
readings.en: like a vine and like a flower in a pomegranate
readings.plain: like a vine and like a flower on a pomegranate tree

why: 'In your blood' is the only Hebrew reading, and it repeats the phrase of 16:6, 22. But it does not make a clear picture of a vine. Codex Vaticanus seems to have read a different Hebrew word (rimmon 'pomegranate'), and commentators have proposed other changes, such as 'in your vineyard' or 'in your likeness'. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and says here that it is hard.
